findings: Single lateral radiograph of the distal leg, ankle, and foot showing the distal tibia and fibula, tibiotalar (ankle) joint, talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and the metatarsal bases with overlapping metatarsal shafts typical of a lateral foot projection. Bone cortices of the tibia, fibula, and tarsal bones appear continuous on both the grayscale and edge-enhanced images, without a visible fracture line, cortical step-off, or displacement. The ankle (tibiotalar) joint space appears preserved and there is no gross malalignment or dislocation. Trabecular bone pattern appears unremarkable with no focal lytic or sclerotic lesion identified. A faint transverse lucent band near the distal tibial metaphysis is visible on the zoomed and contrast-enhanced views, most consistent with a normal open growth plate (physis), suggesting a skeletally immature patient rather than a fracture. No definite soft tissue swelling is appreciated, though soft tissue detail is limited by the bone-optimized processing and image contrast. Faint vertical banding artifact is present in the background across all versions of the image, consistent with a detector/plate or compression artifact rather than a clinical finding.
impression: No definite acute fracture, dislocation, or focal osseous lesion identified on this single lateral view of the ankle and foot. The lucency near the distal tibial metaphysis most likely represents a normal physis (growth plate) in a skeletally immature patient rather than a fracture line, but this cannot be fully confirmed from a single projection. Overall appearance is most consistent with a normal/unremarkable lateral ankle-foot radiograph.
limitations: Only a single lateral projection was provided; a standard trauma series (AP and mortise/oblique views) is needed to reliably exclude subtle or non-displaced fractures, particularly given overlapping bones in the midfoot/forefoot on this view. Image processing (contrast enhancement, sharpening, edge detection) was used only to aid visualization and was cross-checked against the original image; no processing artifact was interpreted as pathology. Soft tissue detail is limited due to bone-focused windowing. No clinical history, patient age, or symptoms were available to correlate with the imaging findings. This analysis is intended as a second-opinion support tool and does not replace formal interpretation by a qualified radiologist or treating physician.
